Eggs of the Long-billed thrasher incubated under controlled conditions at 36 °C [T = 36 °C] exhibit a developmental period leading to hatching after approximately 13.5 days [ab = approximately 13.5 days], a value derived from observations on the congeneric Curve-billed thrasher, Toxostoma curvirostre. Upon emergence, neonatal chicks are altricial and weigh just 5.60 grams [Wwb = 5.60 grams], a modest initial mass that underscores the substantial parental investment required during the subsequent brooding and provisioning phases. This hatchling mass is comparable to that reported for other medium-sized mimids and reflects the energetic constraints of egg production in a species that invests in multiple nesting attempts per season. The altricial nestlings develop rapidly under the constant warmth of the incubating adult.

Under the thermal conditions typical of an active adult bird, approximately 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], the developmental schedule for the Long-billed thrasher progresses through well-defined juvenile milestones. Fledging, defined as the achievement of first flight and nest departure, is recorded at 13 days after birth [tx = 13 days after birth], a value consistent with that reported for the congeneric Brown thrasher, Toxostoma rufum at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This early departure from the nest marks the transition to a fledgling stage where the young bird remains dependent on parental provisioning while developing flight proficiency. Following fledging, the juvenile bird enters a period of rapid somatic growth and behavioral maturation.

Sexual maturation in the Long-billed thrasher is a comparatively rapid process under the standard temperature regime of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. Puberty, defined by the onset of gonadal activity and gametogenesis, has been estimated to occur at approximately 39 days after birth [tp = approximately 39 days after birth], a value inferred from life-history data for the related Brown thrasher, Toxostoma rufum at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This relatively early attainment of reproductive maturity allows individuals to potentially breed during their first full breeding season if conditions are favorable. However, first reproduction is typically deferred until the subsequent season. The pre-reproductive juvenile phase is characterized by continued feather development and the refinement of foraging skills necessary for nutritional independence.

The initiation of a breeding adult's first reproductive effort occurs after a considerable period of somatic development. The time since birth at first brood has been documented at 330 days [tR = 330 days] and this period is measured from birth when maintained under a metabolic reference temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This delay between the attainment of puberty and actual first reproduction suggests that ecological factors, such as territory establishment and mate acquisition, impose significant constraints on reproductive scheduling. Breeding adults typically produce approximately 2 to 3 clutches each year [F_R_i = approximately 2 to 3 clutches each year], with each clutch containing two to five eggs [N_R_i = each clutch containing two to five eggs]. This reproductive output is characteristic of many temperate-zone passerines.

Maximum longevity in this species has been estimated at 7.8 years [am = 7.8 years] when considering a standard active metabolic temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. Fully grown adult individuals ultimately attain an asymptotic body mass of 67.65 grams [Wwi = 67.65 grams], a value that reflects the species' position within the mimid body-size continuum. This ultimate wet weight is achieved through a prolonged period of mass gain during the juvenile and sub-adult stages. The combination of a relatively high annual reproductive output with a moderate lifespan suggests a life-history strategy adapted to variable environmental conditions, where the capacity for repeated nesting attempts buffers against periodic nest failure typical of open-cup nesting passerines in scrubland habitats.
